rationale: B wins because it turns the announcement's weakest proof point into a real story: "Databricks graded its own model, and that is the part enterprises should check." A is strong, but it keeps that same issue in the utility drawer with "independent (not company-run) benchmark numbers before any capability claim goes in a pitch" instead of making it a beat-shaped accountability angle. Both sets understand the finance and regulated-enterprise plays; B gives the founder one more usable route to coverage without padding the deck.
gaps_in_A: "Is open-source the new enterprise-AI land grab? A big vendor is now giving the model away to sell everything around it" outruns the supplied facts; the update does not say what Databricks sells around the model or prove a broader land grab.
"frontier-quality models for enterprises arrive as closed hosted APIs" smuggles in a capability altitude the update does not support; the benchmarks are explicitly company-run.

A treats the benchmark issue as only a proof caveat: "independent (not company-run) benchmark numbers before any capability claim goes in a pitch." That is also a legitimate reporter angle, and A leaves it on the table.
gaps_in_B: "open weights mean third parties can begin reproducing them immediately" is a shade too asserted; the update says open-sourced/open license, but not the exact artifact, access mechanics, or reproduction conditions.
"the period the 60% growth covers" is over-lawyered because the update already says year over year; the sharper ask is which fiscal period and what revenue definition.
"category-creation" is venture-boardroom labeling. The underlying monetization angle works, but that tag smells like a deck, not a newsroom.
